sections.heading: Harnesses that survive a crash

tweets.text:
Much like we did with @aisdk, we're bringing a truly open-source, runtime-agnostic solution to harness durability.

We're extending the durability infra that powers @eve and Workflows to all harnesses, like Pi and OpenCode. Local, Vercel, or DIY.

Fun fact: even Claude Code and Codex can be made durable (and observable!) this way. The catch: they're not (currently) designed for embedding, which makes them less efficient, less portable, and brings an extra sandbox requirement compared to Pi or Fx.

sections.heading: Cost per accepted task

tweets.text:
interesting data from my most recent 2000 real tasks

all of these tasks' outcome got accepted by me, so consider them all successful. when a model didn't give me good results, i would get it to do more iterations until it succeeded

the main caveat is the "plan" bucket - if i didn't like a model's plan, i would sometimes just abandon it and it wouldn't show up here. sometimes i also explicitly ask astra / fable for difficult plans. so take the plan row with a grain of salt. the other rows are mostly randomized and fair

reasoning effort was set at xhigh for plan, medium for others

explaining the task types:
- research: these are mostly answering my questions
- plan: these are technical planning. it could be designing a new feature, or reproducing a bug
- implement: implementing an already defined spec
- fix: fix a bug that's already reproduced

a few interesting signals:

- sol 6.1 and sonnet 5.5 are almost exact equivalents, and they are both 5-10x more efficient at my implement and fix tasks than opus and astra

- grok 4.7 is efficient at read-only tasks, but quite expensive for writing code - this is likely because of its high price point for cached tokens so long coding sessions become very costly

- astra is a lot more expensive than opus 5.5, despite its token efficiency advantage. this is awkward because if sonnet matches sol, opus is better than astra, fable 5.5 is coming, and openai's subscription's $ value is getting cut in half, how do they compete?

Day 16/

You can now cache for 12h in the API and for logged in users across Codex & Work we keep cache forever and you don’t have any penalty for coming back to an old conversation or resuming after a few hours and are now guaranteed to hit the cache. https://t.co/0HYeB01KVh

sections.body: Kun bucketed 2000 accepted tasks by type (research, plan, implement, fix) and found big **cost gaps per bucket** between models. OpenAI now caches for **12h in the API** and keeps cache indefinitely for signed-in Codex users.

detail.tldr: **Meta** is building **Confidential VMs for Muse on the web** — an encrypted environment even Meta can't see into, subscriber-gated at first (verified, TestingCatalog). **GPT-6.1 Terra** surfaced in a merged **Microsoft EF Core PR** (18 eval configs switched judges, verified via LuminaBench). **Google** open-sourced **AQuA**, a watchdog agent for production AI (**Apache 2.0**). tldrBullets: Muse Confidential VMs: encrypted web env where **even Meta can't access** your chats/data; **Meta AI subscribers first**; no voice/image/video/wearables at launch; Meta had teased before-end-2026

GPT-6.1 Terra: model ID **gpt-6.1-terra** appeared in **merged Microsoft EF Core PR #39217** (Oct 16) — 18 eval configs switched from GPT-5.6 Terra to 6.1 as default judge (task model: GPT-6.1 Sol); The Information also reported a new Terra in the works

Google AQuA (**Ambient Quality Agent**): open-source **ADK recipe** in **google/adk-recipes** under **Apache 2.0** — sweeps prod traces from Cloud Trace/Logging/BigQuery, clusters failures, diagnoses root causes; runs **beside** the agent, never in the request path

Free “ESRI” = **QGIS**: free open-source GIS, **200+ native processing algorithms**, raster/vector/mesh/point-cloud, export to image/PDF/SVG, near-complete ESRI symbology (post didn't name it; identification is from the verbatim feature description)

sections.heading: Audit the last 24 hours

tweets.text:
sharing a very high value loop i run everyday at 3am

"audit my development work in the last 24h, identify bottlenecks that slowed down my velocity, and propose improvements"

it feels great to see your work gets smoother every day

sections.heading: One pinned session, many subagents

tweets.text:
i'm doing a bunch of work on our desktop app

my flow is a single pinned "gooey" session where i tell it to do all work in subagents

then as i use it i keep telling it ideas/fixes i want and it goes off in a subagent to implement them - these can even be in different worktrees if it's complicated

it'll pop open html documents with screenshots to communicate before/after and give me options to pick

because a lot is going on in parallel i often will ask "what do you need from me" so it tells me what is ready for review

I think most people multi-tasking with agents could benefit from slowing down

most of the stuff you're doing wont really matter- what's your P0? what would it look like if you gave it your full attention?

a weird thing about OSS pull requests these days is we don't know what model was used for it and our internal setup provides better tools to the agent

so they're almost always worse than sending the prompt ourselves

it's mostly useful for environments we cannot recreate

sections.body: Dax keeps a single **pinned session** that sends each idea to a subagent (in its own worktree if needed), shows before/after HTML with screenshots, and answers "what do you need from me". Thariq's counterweight: name your **P0** and give it full attention.

sections.heading: Harness first, then context

tweets.text:
had a lot of fun talking with @HarryStebbings about all things ai

one line of questioning we went done - vertical vs horizontal agents, and how to build them

im bullish on vertical agents, and i think you can create differentiation (from horizontal agents) in three ways:

1/ context: prompts, skills, tools - all of this is specific to your domain, pretty easy to provide, and gives domain specific context to the agent

2/ harness: harder to tweak than context, but can alter fundemental behavior of the agent

3/ model: hardest to tweak of all, but obviously changes behavior greatly

i think most agent engineers these days are still tweaking 1 and 2 (in that order)

nb: regardless of what layer you tweak at, as the base models change you should revisit your context/harness/model every 3-6 months (and generally remove cruft that is no longer needed)

https://t.co/gmA8oyfxiX

Would agree with this

Start with a harness (I like deepagents)

Add context (skills, tools)

Then if needed modify harness slightly (middleware in deepagents is goated for this)

Then if needed make workflow with langgraph https://t.co/x2qTscyehR

ironically, LLMs themselves have NOT internalized the bitter lesson

when using LLMs to write LLM powered systems, they keep building rigid knowledge with deterministic code, and don’t know where to cut the line of writing prompts instead

sections.body: Harrison's order: start from a **harness**, add skills and tools, tweak the harness, and only then build a graph; revisit all three every few months and cut cruft. Kun: LLMs still over-build **deterministic code** where a prompt would do.

You wouldn't believe the hours I spent manually testing and verifying Omarchy releases during the first year. With Prime's stellar work leading the QA effort, we can finally replace all that toil with agents 🤘 https://t.co/QWqzQWXzfB

The latest Rex preview release includes a very important subsystem I've been working on for weeks to enable full forwards+backwards API compatibility with clients and servers. This was gating the Linux test program and massively opening up the Mac test program. 

We just invited another 1,000 (to Mac) and if it goes well this will step up considerably this week. The Linux test program will likely start this week (separate invite waves amongst existing testers). 

The API compatibility system is super cool. At a high level:

Every API change is a rule on a JSON pointer (RFC 6901). 

For each message, we compile all the rules between your version and ours into a trie keyed by JSON path tokens. This happens lazily since we don't want a full quadratic explosion (a message with N revisions has N possible chains of length 1 to N). We don't want to build N^2/2 trie nodes when most WON'T be visited.

Next, we wrote a custom recursive descent streaming JSON editor (forward-pass only). If a key doesn't match any subtree in the trie, we fast-path copy the full value onto the wire (nothing in it can possibly matter for compatibility). 

Equal chains of changes are interned to the same pointer, so when we broadcast an event to many old clients, we translate it once per distinct chain, not once per client.

The result of all this plus some other work is that we simulated various shapes of 10,000 long revision chains (note: we're on revision 4 at the moment...) with pathological changes of various shapes and an upgrade costs about 35 _microseconds_ on a 20KB JSON body.

sections.heading: Prove it, don't just test it

tweets.text:
pstack v0.15.27 ships with a new skill /create-formal-verification-skill! 

it's still in beta, and similar to /create-verification-skill, this is a meta-skill that creates a new skill and formal verification suite based on the characteristics you want to verify. for example, you may want to model state machines and systems with concurrency using TLA+, or use kani in rust to check for undefined behavior. 

if you're new to formal verification, think of it as mathematically proving properties and invariants (something that must always be true) or "laws" of your system. usually, this means modeling your programs in a separate language like with TLA+ and then running the solver on that spec. newer approaches like with kani and @bendlang take a different approach where there is no separate language: you write kani in rust, and bend in bend (it's also a programming language, and the proofs are written as laws and expressed in its type system).

historically formal verification never reached mainstream status because of the difficulty in modeling and writing proofs. it's quite difficult to model your business requirements and keep them in sync! but i expect that we will see more innovation in formal verification in the future as being able to formally verifiy that the code does what you intended gives your agents superpowers in writing correct software.

in the meantime though, i've been experimenting with modeling our code with TLA+ and have already found several bugs with the skill created by /create-formal-verification-skill. 

try it out and let me know how it goes!

Give your agent a way to verify its work. This can dramatically improve the quality of output.

With this process in place, Claude Code was able to write 90%+ of its code itself. When generating software at a faster rate than you can review it, the bottleneck shifts to proving that it works. @bcherny and team invested enough in verification, we've been able to move fast while maintaining stability.

Code reviews aren't going away, but you need to think of it differently. One human reading through line-by-line is no longer going to work as a gate, it needs to evolve into a multi-layered verification system, built with fast deterministic feedback loops for your agents. 

This is where e2e tests, feature maps (as @poteto has been advocating), property tests and multi-agent adversarial reviews come in. These all provide opportunities to catch errors early and fix them before things get out of hand.

You don't have enough eyeballs for the amount of code being written so your focus needs to be on product intent, risk assessment and evaluating evidence rather than reviewing code. Delegate the code checking work to your automated tests, scale your approvals based on risk, and turn your test failures into living evaluations. This approach helps maintain speed without losing reliability.

Let the agents do what they do best and let you focus on what makes you irreplaceable: judgement, direction, and ownership. We tried to capture how we handle code review and verification in this writeup. Hopefully it's helpful.

recommended reading. i like the term "coherence" over "taste".

historically, simplified, a human would approach a software writing human, asking them to build a thing. that's an iterative process, until software writing human truely understands what the other human needs and wants. which is also why we moved away from waterfall. you often can't know what you want before you've build a first shitty solution you can feel out. and your wants might change.

in this scenario, the outcome is what matters, not the program structure itself, unless that makes the outcome worse/impossible (bugs, perf, ease of adding features). 

the software writing human's skill is not so much programming itself, but understanding the other humans wants, pulling out domain knowledge from the other human, asking questions, and ultimately translating the other human's wants into programs, while ensuring the program structure is fit to be modified for future needs.

now, can you replace the software writing human with an agent? for simple one-off stuff, yes. if the human with a want is technically minded that extends to more complex programs. 

most humans suuuuuck at this iterative colab with agents tho, as they are bad at structuring and communicating their wants. 

and agents currently still suck at the software writing human skill of colaborating with another human to understand their wants and translate them to a program.

my gut tells me that this is because the training data and RL for coding agent tasks is largely composed of trajectories where a software writing human and an agent colaborate. that missed the other half of the problem: the human with a want and software writing human interaction.

and until we can encode that agents for writing programs will likely only be effective in the hands of software writing humans, or very technically minded humans.

another thing agents currently suck ar is translating software writing human shallow instructions into architecture that's not a house of cards. i think this too is a consequence of the lack of training data/RL-able trajectories that encode the process a team of software writing humans go through when building a thing. we do have digitized artifacts (design docs, commits/PRs, issue trackers) that capture some but not all of that.

i think this will improve, as we all are now doing design sessions with our agents, so labs could in theory train on that. however, even if this data were available and becomes part of training, the pretraining data still has tons of shit code from around the internet in it, ehich posttraining would have to combat.

sections.heading: Comments are weeds

tweets.text:
ban and delete most if not all code comments!

agents love copying what already exists. a seemingly harmless comment explaining some temporary workaround is one of the worst viruses you can have in your codebase. like a weed it'll spread quickly as a tool for agents to quickly get their job done. before you know it, your codebase is overrun with hacks and stale comments. just one more workaround bro 

you can use pstack's /no-comments skill as a weedkiller. it'll seek out useless comments while keeping the ones that actually should exist (like explaining a browser quirk), and figure out how to solve them on a first principles basis

here's a prompt you can try asking @bot:

create a project agent that uses /poteto-mode to spawn a /swarm to use /no-comments and identify useless code comments we can prune in my repo. come back with a high level plan of which of these workarounds would be best solved by refactoring and which we can straight up delete

https://t.co/nqeRdY62ee

• comments go stale very quickly and confuse agents and people
• they are often used by agents to explain workarounds that would've been better off actually fixing the code instead
• they are not enforceable and waste your agents' tokens

my point is that moving prose (comments, rules, agent.md, skills) into deterministic lint rules, better API design/types, is far more effective, enforceable, and token efficient.

comments are simply a crutch that agents will happily misuse

this is now a new skill /in-your-own-words in pstack 0.15.23! 

extremely useful to ensure that you and your agent are aligned on the goal and that it understands your intent clearly

sections.heading: How subagents report back

tweets.text:
we are thinking a lot about how to make deepagents more async native. specifically about making async subagents work better/more prominent

one key question is how does a finished subagent "notify" the parent agent? some default behaviors we're considering for when the parent is still running:

1/ interrupt parent run, apply subagent update, continue (basically same as "steer")

2/ wait for parent run to finish, then batch subagent update with any other new messages (basically same as "queue")

another question is how to handle human in the loop? what if main agent is not running but paused and waiting explicit human response to an action?

a/ wait for human to respond, then batch the subagent update with that

b/ resume thread (which would cancel the human interrupt) with the subagent update (thread could then re-ask for the same human approval)

any other options we're missing?

sections.body: Two defaults on the table for deepagents: **interrupt** the running parent (steer) or **batch** the update after it finishes (queue).

the latest argument is “you just tell your agent what you want, and your agent will vibe code software on the fly to get that done, so no one will need real software any more”

sounds reasonable, until you realize it costs tokens, compute, and wall clock time to build those software on the fly

so instead of one-click launching an app, the bet is people will prefer to write a prompt, wait for 15 minutes, then get something that may or may not do what they want, and at the end of the month pay more $$$ for the token spend, higher than all their software combined

that’s literally the argument

and if we look at the world in aggregate, most people would just end up building the exact same “personal” software repeatedly

oh - your agent just spent 3 days and $500 of tokens vibe coding your terminal multiplexer? mine just did exactly the same! let’s celebrate how personal our terminal multiplexers are!

sorry - i just don’t see that as being a happy scenario for anyone, other than people who profit from telling others how to waste $ on tokens

to be constructive, here’s what i believe as the future state -

- high quality software that takes high cost to make will continue to thrive. just like good restaurants don’t compete with your air fryer and microwave 

- most of those software will be offered headlessly for people to use via their agents, and they can continue to monetize such usage. this is already the case with products like jira, linear, stripe

- human-facing software will all offer dynamic UI that can be adjusted with natural language on the fly so they can be personalized easily, but their core doesn’t have to be rebuilt by every user repeatedly

instead of “software is dead”, i believe good software becomes “strong core, headless service, fluid interface”

which future do you think is more likely?

Agent contributions to Omarchy are not only very welcome, but I usually prefer them! Rare is the human who has the patience to match an agent in providing all the pertinent details in a bug report. Also, PRs are mostly just proofs of concept now anyway.

sections.heading: Verification closes the loop
sections.body:
**Lauren** [@poteto](https://x.com/poteto/status/2109436202554372476): start with verification so agents can close the loop, and prefer artifacts (video, screenshots) that are **easier to review than the whole PR**.

**Addy** [@addyosmani](https://x.com/addyosmani/status/2109358790298787931): define **done** before review, give the agent checks it can run, then ship when nothing blocks.

**Matt** [@mattpocockuk](https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2109589900706083024): don't blame the agent for a bad test; blame the codebase that allowed it.

tweets.text:
okay now that we're past that tired discussion, let's talk about how we get agents to write more correct code (note: this won't mean the code will be Good, but it should at least work)

this is the entrypoint into your most basic agentic loop: verification. it means giving your agent the ability to verify its own work, most commonly by actually running and interacting with it like a real user would. whether your interface is a cli/api/ui/whatever, you want to start here so that your agents can close the loop. if you want you can even have your agents model the problem in TLA+ and attempt to verify if you have things like state machine bugs.

the point is to give yourself confidence in the agents' work by them producing some kind of artifact that proves that 1) that the work is correct, 2) that it matches what you intended, and 3) is easier to review than reading the whole PR. most commonly this would be a video and/or screenshots for UI work.

everything else like skill packs are really bonus and optional, all you need is a way for your agents to verify their own work to start using them more autonomously. some caveats are that not all domains can be verified easily yet, and that verification is just approximation and can still be wrong. it's no different than trusting that a human actually ran the code they wrote and trusting it

so start here!

Verification is one of the most important things for getting great results out of your agent.

Clearly define "done" before code review starts. 
A reviewer, human or agent, asked to find bugs without this may still find something that could be improved. 

Give Claude checks it can run (bash commands, tests, clicking through the app in a browser) and have it pass that too before it says it's finished. 

When nothing blocks merge and ship.

Don't blame the agent for writing the bad test

Blame the codebase for allowing the bad test to be written

callout.text: Before asking an agent to ship, give it a runnable done check (tests, CLI, or a browser click-through) and require a short evidence artifact.

sections.heading: Evidence, not just diffs
sections.body:
**Addy** [@addyosmani](https://x.com/addyosmani/status/2109384286763958742): agents make checks cheap, so quality comes from **loops the agent can run itself**, and taste compounds when mistakes become shared config, hooks, or tests.

**Matt’s** experimental [`/chief-of-staff`](https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2109314001704194090) skill ran a side-by-side latency comparison against OBS that he says he would never have done himself.

tweets.text:
Agents write code "much better on average at scale" is right. The "at scale" part comes from verification. Agents make checking cheap.

The stuff that made "Good Code" expensive (tests, benchmarks, specs, real e2e runs) is now a cheap thing you can ask an agent for. You can improve the checks.

So our work is less "review every line" and more "build loops the agent can run itself". Give the agent a way to verify the work. That loop is where quality comes from.

And make taste compound. When the agent gets something wrong, write it down (shared config, a hook, a test) so it doesn't happen twice. A human still owns what ships but now they're reviewing evidence and not just diffs.

Having a pretty fun time with Opus this weekend

My (experimental) /chief-of-staff skill is trying to replace OBS with a homebrew video recorder.

So it's running a side-by-side latency comparison where it has asked me to:

1. Download a video it made itself to my phone
2. Prop it up and show it to my camera
3. Point my microphone at it
4. Simultaneously record my screen and play sounds
5. Check all available inputs for latency
6. Compare against OBS and my own setup

Truly bonkers levels of verification and I freaking love it, I would never be this thorough if I were developing this myself

sections.heading: Tests as source of truth
sections.body:
**Kun Chen** [@kunchenguid](https://x.com/kunchenguid/status/2108030810691629403) published a DeepSWE eval takeaway: telling Sonnet 5.5 high **not to write unit/integration tests** produced a slightly higher success rate (not statistically significant) with **statistically significant less time and tokens**.

Across the “tests allowed” arm, ~65% unit / ~35% integration, **neither bucket beat writing no tests**. Disabling execution of existing tests on a ==44-task== sample also didn’t move success.

His read: agent-written tests often **restate the same interpretation of intent** as the implementation, so they aren’t an independent oracle. He caveated e2e (almost none were written in that eval) and said he’ll run a dedicated e2e study.

In follow-ups he stressed human steering, and that useful tests need **absolute authority assigned by humans** ([thread reply](https://x.com/kunchenguid/status/2108069278914392460)).

**Geoffrey Huntley** [@GeoffreyHuntley](https://x.com/GeoffreyHuntley/status/2108054698213396821) strongly disagreed, arguing agent-authored **mutation and property-based tests** make a real regression harness. **Matt Pocock**, in replies, cooled on enforcing strict TDD while still valuing tests.

callout.text: Agent-written tests tend to repeat the implementation’s own reading of intent, so they **aren’t an independent check**. Kun’s take: humans decide which tests carry authority.

tweets.text:
ok it's official... AI-written unit tests and integration tests are empirically proven to be unhelpful. you should tell your agents to stop writing tests by themselves

on the deepswe eval set, banning sonnet 5.5 high from writing any tests actually resulted in slightly higher success rate (non stat-sig), with less time and token spent (stat-sig). this is pretty hard empirical evidence

across the tests that were written by the "tests allowed" baseline arm, 65% of them were unit tests, 35% were integration tests, neither bucket resulted in any improvement compared to not writing any tests at all

i also picked a random sample of 44 tasks subset where i completely disabled executing even existing tests - it also did not affect success rate at all

i spot checked many tests written in the baseline arm, and my intuition is that most tests are simply a repetition of the implementation

agent-written tests do not add any value because both the implementation and the tests were simply the agent's interpretation of our intent. the tests aren't any more accurate than the implementation itself

i suspect we can still extract some value from unit tests and integration tests if we describe them ourselves when we believe we can articulate our intent better through test cases than through requirements. but i have not proven this yet

also worth noting, during deepswe eval the agent wrote almost no e2e tests (only 17, compared to 3000+ unit/integration tests written). so this analysis does not prove nor disprove the value of e2e tests - i will do another eval specifically for that

STRONG strong disagree. mutation testing, property based testing authored by agents create a really really good safety harness that helps with verification, correctness and ensuring future increments do not cause regressions.

cards.title: Dogwood temporal policies: govern the sequence, not one call
cards.body: AgentCore Policy now evaluates session history with Dogwood (Cedar-compatible): require prior approval, cap cumulative spend, enforce step order — at the Gateway, outside agent code. Pass x-amzn-bedrock-agentcore-policy-session-id; start LOG_ONLY then ENFORCE.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · Aug 6, 2026 · AgentCore Policy temporal docs

detail.summary: Most agent guardrails judge each tool call alone. That misses the failure modes SAs actually hear about: a transfer after looking up a different account, many small purchases under a per-call limit, or a retry loop that burns tokens overnight. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds temporal policies — session-aware rules written in Dogwood (open source, Cedar-compatible) and enforced on the Gateway — so the policy engine looks at what the agent already did in that session before allowing the next hop. Pair with Gateway rate limits (RPS/RPM/TPM/connections) for cost ceilings that do not live in prompts.

sections.heading: Why this is an SA narrative
sections.body: Stateless Cedar/Gateway policies answer “can this principal call this tool with these inputs?” Temporal policies answer “given what already happened in this session, should this next action be allowed?” That is the difference between trusting the agent and knowing the boundary holds across a multi-step trajectory. Enforcement sits in infrastructure: the agent never sees the Dogwood logic and cannot prompt its way around it. Decisions stay deny-by-default, deterministic, and logged with full context.

sections.heading: Dogwood operators you will teach
sections.body: Dogwood embeds Cedar, so existing point-in-time policies keep working. Add a temporal { } block only where history matters. Core operators: formerly within (a matching prior event in a window), since within (a condition has held since an anchor), plus count and sum aggregations. Example pattern from docs: permit SellShares only when a matching ApproveSale response occurred within 1h with the same stock/shares and output.approved == true. Quotas to remember: 20 temporal policies per engine, 3 temporal operators per policy, max 24h window per condition.

sections.heading: Session ID is your design knob
sections.body: You generate the session ID (recommend UUIDv4) and send it on every Gateway request as x-amzn-bedrock-agentcore-policy-session-id. The Gateway does not mint one for you. Omit it while any temporal policy is attached and requests fail validation. Idle timeout is 24h from last activity. Prefer per-conversation sessions; use per-user only when you need cross-conversation budgets; never use per-request (that disables history). Authenticated gateways (CUSTOM_JWT / AWS_IAM) bind session to caller identity so two callers cannot share a stream by copying an ID.

sections.heading: Multi-hop + IAM gotchas
sections.body: On Gateway → Runtime → Gateway chains in the same account and Region, AgentCore propagates identity via a Workload Access Token (WAT) on an internal header — your agent code must not set or strip it. Temporal sessions do not cross accounts or Regions; keep Gateway and targets co-located. Gateway role needs bedrock-agentcore:GetWorkloadAccessToken even when outbound auth is IAM. Changing temporal policies on an engine invalidates open sessions (next reuse → HTTP 409); start a fresh session ID after policy edits.

sections.heading: Ship safely this week
sections.body: Author one temporal rule that matches a customer story (approval-before-transfer, max N transfers/session, or block external notify after PHI read). Attach it in LOG_ONLY, exercise happy/unhappy paths with a fixed session ID, then promote to ENFORCE. Layer Gateway rate limits (per-caller RPM + per-target TPM + connection caps) as the cost backstop — remember rate limits fail-open if the limiter is down, so they are not your sole security boundary. Document Region availability (e.g. us-east-1 / us-west-2 yes; us-west-1 no) before customer designs.

cards.title: Bedrock Managed Agents (OpenAI) now in preview
cards.body: AWS + OpenAI shipped Bedrock Managed Agents (BMA) in preview Sep 29: AWS-native agent sessions with IAM roles, durable state, skills, MCP tools, human-approval hooks, and CloudTrail — run on self-hosted exec or AgentCore Runtime. Preview: no extra BMA fee beyond underlying resources; us-east-1 / us-west-2 / us-east-2.
cards.source: AWS What's New · Sep 29, 2026 · Bedrock Managed Agents docs

detail.summary: On Sep 29, 2026 AWS announced Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents (BMA), powered by OpenAI, in public preview. Built jointly with OpenAI on a customized Agents API that is AWS-native, BMA lets you run OpenAI-optimized agents entirely inside AWS with the identities, permissions, and governance you already use. The service manages state, tool selection, code execution, and multi-step coordination; you supply instructions, an IAM role, tools/skills/MCP servers, and an execution environment (self-hosted exec server or AgentCore Runtime). Preview pricing: no additional charge for BMA beyond the AWS resources agents consume (subject to change at GA). Regions at launch: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio).

sections.heading: Why SAs should care
sections.body: Customers keep asking for OpenAI-class agent loops without leaving AWS identity and audit boundaries. BMA is the preview answer: each agent session gets its own IAM role, optional human approval before consequential actions, CloudTrail on supported API activity, and durable sessions that retain messages, tool calls, and intermediate results so work can pause and resume. Position it next to AgentCore Runtime/Gateway — not as a replacement for every agent framework, but as the managed OpenAI harness path when governance and AWS-native tooling matter more than DIY orchestration.

sections.heading: What BMA owns vs what you own
sections.body: BMA runs the agent loop (model ↔ tools), preserves session state, and can compact context as conversations grow. You choose the execution environment where commands and local tools actually run: (1) self-hosted — your host/container with a running exec server; or (2) AgentCore Runtime — managed microVM sessions in your account, under an execution role you control, optionally VPC-connected. Model calls stay with Bedrock Managed Agents; the environment only runs the commands the agent sends. Skills are reusable procedure packs; MCP servers plug in extra tools.

sections.heading: Security shape to teach
sections.body: Docs call out three identities: the caller, the session role BMA assumes (role_arn), and the execution-environment identity. Keep them separate and least-privilege. Callers need iam:PassRole on the session role; AgentCore paths also need bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime / StopRuntimeSession scoped to your Runtime ARNs. Commands and MCP tools inherit whatever the execution environment can reach — use a dedicated workspace and restricted OS identity. Preview signing service is bedrock-mantle on regional endpoints; session path is under /openai/v1/agents/sessions.

sections.heading: Where it fits an SA narrative
sections.body: Good demo/story arcs: multi-step codebase investigation, document processing, or file generation where durable sessions + skills beat one-shot chat. Contrast with Strands/AgentCore harness (any model/framework) vs BMA (OpenAI-optimized, AWS-governed). Call out preview caveats: APIs may change before GA, pricing can change, and model availability differs by Region/account — always verify current Regional availability before customer designs.

cards.title: India NRE interest: India-free ≠ US-free
cards.body: US citizens and residents must report worldwide bank interest — including India NRE/NRO/FCNR interest — on Form 1040 even when India treats NRE interest as tax-free for NRIs. No Form 1099 from the Indian bank does not mean skip it; list payers on Schedule B and answer the foreign-account questions. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Pub. 550 · Pub. 17 · Schedule B (Form 1040)

detail.summary: Publication 550 (Investment Income and Expenses) and Publication 17 remind U.S. citizens that foreign-source investment income — including interest from banks outside the United States — must be reported on the U.S. return unless a specific U.S. law or treaty exemption applies. Indian NRE accounts are often marketed as tax-free interest under Indian rules for non-resident Indians; that India-side result does not create a U.S. exclusion. If you are a U.S. citizen or resident alien (green card or substantial presence), include the USD equivalent of NRE/NRO/FCNR interest on Form 1040 line 2b, usually via Schedule B. This tip is educational only and is not tax, legal, or investment advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin U.S. citizens, green-card holders, and substantial-presence residents who still hold India NRE, NRO, or FCNR deposits (or recently flipped from NRI status). Especially relevant if a bank or relative said NRE interest is tax-free without distinguishing India vs. U.S. rules, or if you never received a Form 1099-INT from the Indian bank and assumed nothing was reportable.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Pub. 550 foreign-source-income reminder: report foreign investment income whether you live in the U.S. or abroad and whether or not a Form 1099 arrives. Convert credited interest to USD with a consistent FX method, list each foreign payer and amount on Schedule B Part I (Interest), and carry the total to Form 1040 line 2b. Schedule B Part III asks whether you had a financial interest in or signature authority over a foreign account — answer Yes for India bank accounts and complete FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR) / Form 8938 when those separate thresholds apply (they do not replace reporting the interest as income). If India actually withheld tax on NRO interest, you may explore a Foreign Tax Credit on Form 1116; NRE interest that India did not tax usually produces no India credit to offset the U.S. tax.

sections.heading: India angle: NRE myth vs. U.S. worldwide tax
sections.body: India domestic exemption for certain NRE interest for persons treated as non-residents under Indian law is an India statute result. The United States taxes citizens and residents on worldwide income. Becoming a U.S. tax resident (or already being a citizen) while an Indian bank still labels the account NRE is a classic mismatch: the product name does not rewrite IRC worldwide-inclusion rules. Keep passbook / statement interest totals for the calendar year even if the statement shows zero TDS.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: Pull 2025 (and YTD 2026) interest credited on every India NRE/NRO/FCNR account, convert to USD, and draft Schedule B payer lines before you file. Separately confirm FBAR (aggregate foreign accounts over $10,000 anytime in the year) and Form 8938 thresholds — reporting the account is not the same as omitting the interest.

sections.heading: Educational label
sections.body: Educational only — not tax advice. Treaty claims, dual-status years, bona fide residence / physical presence exclusions (earned income, not bank interest), PFIC issues inside India mutual funds, and state tax conformity can change the filing. Confirm with a cross-border tax professional before filing or amending.

cards.title: The 4% rule: spend without running dry
cards.body: Once you have an invested nest egg, a rough sustainable withdrawal is about 4% a year — so $1M funds ~$40k. Treat it as a planning guardrail, not a guarantee.
cards.source: JL Collins · The Simple Path to Wealth (via tiagom87 notes)

detail.summary: Collins (and the broader FIRE literature) uses the 4% rule as a simple starting point for sustainable withdrawals from a diversified portfolio: withdraw roughly 4% of the starting balance in year one, then adjust for inflation. It is a planning tool with room for error — not a promise that markets will cooperate.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body: Financial independence is not only about accumulating; it is about knowing how much you can safely spend without depleting the pile. The 4% heuristic says: take about four percent of your invested nest egg in the first year of withdrawals. On $1 million that is about $40,000. Lower rates (around 3–3.5%) buy more safety; slightly higher rates need flexibility if markets are rough.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body: Historically, broad stock indexes have delivered roughly ~7% real returns over long stretches (about ~10% nominal minus inflation). A 4% withdrawal leaves a cushion for volatility, fees, and bad sequence-of-returns luck — while still letting compounding work on what stays invested. Collins pairs this with a simple index-fund path so the math stays boring on purpose.

sections.heading: Try today
sections.body: Write your current annual spending (or a lean target). Multiply by 25 — that is the rough nest-egg size if you plan on ~4% withdrawals ($40k spend → ~$1M). Then decide whether you want more buffer (multiply by ~30 for ~3.3%). One number on paper beats vague “someday rich.”

detail.summary: Continuous (online) evaluation on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples live agent sessions from CloudWatch logs and scores them with built-in or custom evaluators (Correctness, Faithfulness, Tool-Selection Accuracy, Response Relevance, and more). Because each sampled session invokes an LLM-as-judge, judge cost scales with session volume and SamplingPercentage. The Aug 31, 2026 AWS ML Blog on observable Managed Knowledge Base agentic retrieval explicitly warns that SamplingPercentage: 100 in the sample templates is for the blog experiment only — not a production recommendation. SAs writing Bedrock agent blogs should teach the on-demand → modest continuous pattern and name the single knob: OnlineEvaluationConfig.Rule.SamplingConfig.SamplingPercentage (0.01–100; console default 10%).

sections.heading: Why SAs should care
sections.body: Agentic retrieval (multi-KB routing + AgenticRetrieveStream + reason-and-act loops) makes quality harder to eyeball. Online evaluation closes that gap by scoring live traffic automatically — but copying a demo’s 100% sampling into a busy Runtime turns quality monitoring into a second inference bill. Architecture blogs and Well-Architected reviews need the cost-governance sentence up front: pick a sampling rate that fits budget and policy, then raise it only when you need denser regression signal.

sections.heading: On-demand vs continuous
sections.body: On-demand evaluation is deliberate and finite: you run AgentCore Evaluate (LLM-as-judge) over chosen sessions (or a notebook/driver) and pay only when you kick it off — ideal for development, pre-release gates, and gold-set checks. Continuous (online) evaluation fits production monitoring: AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig samples live sessions and scores them without a manual job. Common pattern from the blog: lean on on-demand while iterating, then enable continuous at a modest sampling percentage once real users are on the Runtime.

sections.heading: The one property that sets the bill
sections.body: In CloudFormation / CreateOnlineEvaluationConfig, set rule.samplingConfig.samplingPercentage (number from 0.01 to 100). The AgentCore console Create online evaluation flow defaults Sampling to 10%. The Aug 31 sample sets 100% so every session is scored immediately for demos — tune templates/03-agent-runtime.yaml (or UpdateOnlineEvaluationConfig) before any production promote. Remember CLI/SDK units carefully: some helpers take a 0–100 percentage; confirm whether 1.0 means 1% or 100% for the API you call.

sections.heading: Pair with observability, not instead of it
sections.body: The same Managed-KB + AgentCore Gateway pattern ships seven telemetry layers (KB metrics, ingestion, retrieval quality, Gateway/MCP, OTEL spans, tokens, evaluation scores). SamplingPercentage only gates Layer-7 continuous scoring cost; you still want L1–L6 for latency, tool health, and token spend. Filters on the evaluation rule can further narrow which sessions are judged (for example high-latency or specific tool paths) so you spend judge tokens where signal is highest.

sections.heading: Try this week
sections.body: In a non-prod AgentCore Runtime with Observability wired, create an OnlineEvaluationConfig with Builtin.Helpfulness (or Correctness + Faithfulness), set SamplingPercentage to 5–10, drive a known prompt set, and compare CloudWatch GenAI Observability → Evaluations against an on-demand batch on the same sessions. Document the rate, evaluator list, and rollback (disable or lower sampling) for your next Bedrock agent cost/quality blog.

cards.title: Bundle a want with a need
cards.body: Temptation bundling pairs something you crave with something you should do — so the fun cue pulls the useful habit along. Make the need ride with the want.
cards.source: James Clear · Atomic Habits (via lijubjohn book-notes)

detail.summary: Clear's Make It Attractive lever includes temptation bundling: link an action you want to do with an action you need to do. The dopamine of the want makes the need easier to start — and habit stacking can wire them into a sequence.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body: Willpower is unreliable; attractiveness is not. When you only schedule the hard habit alone, it competes with every more-fun option. Temptation bundling removes that fight by making the useful behavior the gateway to (or companion of) something you already enjoy.

sections.heading: A simple formula
sections.body: After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [HABIT I NEED]. After [HABIT I NEED], I will [HABIT I WANT]. Example: after I pour coffee, I will review today's top money move for two minutes; after that review, I will open the podcast or show I like. The want is earned by the need — not the other way around.

sections.heading: Try today
sections.body: Pick one sticky need (a 2-minute money check, a short workout opener, or inbox triage) and one guilt-free want (favorite playlist, coffee shop walk, comics). Write the two-line stack once, put it where you'll see it, and run it once today. Adjust the pair if either part feels forced.

Stack: After current → do need → then get want
Works because the cue for fun also cues the productive action

cards.title: Inherited India flat/shares: §1014 often steps basis up to FMV
cards.body: US citizens and residents who inherit an India flat, plot, or demat shares generally take a new US tax basis equal to fair market value on the date of death under IRC §1014 — so decades of pre-death appreciation often escape US capital gains when you later sell. Lifetime gifts are different (carryover basis). Separately, aggregate foreign bequests over $100k still need Form 3520 Part IV. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Pub. 551 (12/2025) · IRC §1014 · Gifts from foreign person / Form 3520

detail.summary: When a US citizen or resident inherits property from a decedent, Internal Revenue Code section 1014 generally sets the heir’s initial US tax basis at the property’s fair market value (FMV) on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date if the estate elects it). IRS Publication 551 (revised December 2025), Basis of Assets, restates that rule under “Inherited Property.” For Indian-origin families, that often means an India residential flat, ancestral land, or listed/demat shares that rose for decades while parents held them can reset to current FMV for US tax — shrinking (or wiping out) US capital gain on a later sale compared with using the decedent’s old cost. This tip is educational only and is not tax, legal, or investment advice; facts, India succession law, and India capital-gains/TDS rules can change the picture.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: US citizens and green-card / substantial-presence residents who inherit India real estate, demat equity, mutual-fund units, or other capital assets from parents or other nonresident-alien (or US) decedents. Especially useful when the asset appreciated for years in India and you may sell, gift, or convert currency later. Less relevant if you only received cash (basis issues differ) or if you already sold with well-documented basis.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics (§1014 step-up)
sections.body: Per Pub. 551, your basis in inherited property is generally (1) FMV at the date of death, (2) FMV on the alternate valuation date if elected for estate tax, (3) special-use valuation in limited farm/business cases, or (4) other estate-tax consistent values when Schedule A (Form 8971) applies. FMV is the price willing buyer and seller would agree on with knowledge of the facts. Contrast: property received as a lifetime gift usually takes a carryover basis from the donor (with dual-basis rules when FMV is below donor basis) — so dying with appreciated India property often produces a cleaner US capital-gains result than gifting it during life. When you sell, report the disposition on Form 8949 / Schedule D using that stepped-up basis (converted to USD with a consistent FX method). Holding period for inherited property is generally treated as long-term.

sections.heading: India-angle: flats, demat, and Form 3520
sections.body: India location does not by itself deny the §1014 FMV reset for a US person heir — foreign situs assets still need a US basis for US tax. Practical gap: India stamp duty / circle rates may understate true FMV; keep a contemporaneous appraisal, broker comps, or registered-valuer report dated near death for your US file. India may still tax the sale under domestic capital-gains rules and withhold TDS; US tax then interacts via the Foreign Tax Credit (Form 1116) — a separate analysis. Reporting is not the same as income tax: if aggregate gifts/bequests from a nonresident alien or foreign estate (plus related foreign persons) exceed $100,000 in the year, file Form 3520 Part IV (IRS “Gifts from foreign person”); purported gifts from foreign corporations/partnerships use the lower inflation-adjusted threshold ($20,573 for 2026). True bequests are generally not US income, but missing 3520 can still draw §6039F penalties.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: If you inherited India property in the last few years (or expect to), collect: death certificate / succession papers, a dated FMV snapshot as of the date of death (appraisal or documented comps), demat/broker statements, and any Form 3520 you filed or still need. Store that packet before you list or transfer the asset so your §1014 basis is evidence-backed.

sections.heading: Educational label
sections.body: Educational only — not tax advice. Anti-abuse exceptions (for example, appreciated property you gifted to the decedent within one year of death), community-property / joint-tenancy basis splits, PFIC stock inside India mutual funds, and covered-expatriate §2801 rules can override the simple story. Confirm with a cross-border tax professional before filing or selling.

cards.title: AgentCore Optimization: recommend from traces, A/B via Gateway
cards.body: Stop guessing prompt fixes. Point AgentCore Recommendations at production OTEL traces + an evaluator (helpfulness, tool selection, etc.), get a system-prompt or tool-description variant, package it as a config bundle, then split live traffic at AgentCore Gateway with p-values before you promote. Preview loop for SAs writing Bedrock agent blogs.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · May 4, 2026 · AgentCore Optimization docs

detail.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Optimization (preview) closes the observe → evaluate → improve loop for production agents. Instead of reading traces by hand and shipping prompt edits blind, you generate Recommendations from AgentCore Observability traces against a chosen evaluator, package the change as an immutable configuration bundle (system prompt, model ID, tool descriptions), validate offline with batch evaluation (or simulated user datasets), then run A/B tests through AgentCore Gateway with online evaluation, confidence intervals, and p-values before promoting the winner. During preview it targets system prompts and tool descriptions for agents on AgentCore Runtime that already use Observability and Evaluations — educational SA pattern, not a production SLA.

sections.heading: Why SAs should care
sections.body: Agent quality drifts daily as models, tools, and user intents shift. The common fix cycle — complaint → skim traces → rewrite prompt → ship — introduces regressions on other sessions. AgentCore Optimization turns that into a data-backed loop SAs can cite in architecture blogs: traces feed recommendations, recommendations become versioned bundles, Gateway splits traffic, Evaluations score both arms with statistical rigor. Pair it with AgentOps pillars (governance, CI/CD, multi-level eval, observability) from the Jun 1, 2026 AgentOps ML Blog.

sections.heading: Recommendations from real traces
sections.body: Call StartRecommendation (type SYSTEM_PROMPT_RECOMMENDATION or TOOL_DESCRIPTION_RECOMMENDATION). Point recommendationConfig at the CloudWatch log group / agent traces, the current system prompt (or tool descriptions), and an evaluationConfig with the reward signal you care about — built-in evaluators such as Builtin.Helpfulness or a custom LLM-as-judge. The service reflects on failure patterns for that evaluator and proposes an optimized variant. Tool-description recommendations sharpen how the model chooses tools without changing tool implementations. You decide what advances to validation.

sections.heading: Configuration bundles vs code changes
sections.body: Bundles are immutable, versioned snapshots keyed by runtime ARN: model ID, system prompt, tool descriptions. Agents read the active bundle dynamically via the AgentCore SDK, so prompt/model swaps are configuration changes — not container redeploys. Use bundle variants on the same Runtime for config-only experiments. For code or framework changes, deploy a second Runtime endpoint and compare via Gateway target-based variants instead.

sections.heading: Validate: batch first, then Gateway A/B
sections.body: Batch evaluation runs the candidate against a curated (or LLM-simulated) dataset and reports aggregate scores so known-good cases do not regress — wire this as a CI gate. Then configure AgentCore Gateway to split live traffic between control and treatment (percentage you set). Online evaluation scores every session; results include confidence intervals and p-values. Promote the winner as the default; pause the test to roll back to the prior configuration. Two variant modes: configuration-bundle variants (same target, W3C baggage injects bundle ref) or target-based variants (different Runtime endpoints).

sections.heading: Try this week
sections.body: In a non-prod account with AgentCore Runtime + Observability + Evaluations enabled, pick Builtin.Helpfulness (or a custom evaluator), run StartRecommendation on a week of failing sessions, create two config bundles (baseline vs recommendation), run batch eval on your gold prompts, then start a low-percentage Gateway A/B before touching production defaults. Document the loop for your next Bedrock agent blog.

detail.summary: On Sep 21, 2026 the Strands Agents team released Strands harness: a batteries-included, general-purpose agent harness (not a coding-only IDE agent) under Apache 2.0. One call to create_harness / createHarness wires a model across Amazon Bedrock (default), Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, or LiteLLM. cards.title: Form 5471: India Pvt Ltd shares can trigger a $10k reporting trap
cards.body: Own (or control) stock in an India private limited company as a US citizen or resident? Form 5471 may be mandatory under IRC §§6038/6046 even when the company paid you nothing — Category 4 if you control >50%, Category 5 if you are a ≥10% US shareholder of a CFC. Miss the attach-to-return deadline and the baseline §6038 penalty is $10,000 per foreign corporation per year. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · About Form 5471 · Instructions for Form 5471 (12/2025) · §§6038/6046

detail.summary: Form 5471 (Information Return of U.S. Persons With Respect To Certain Foreign Corporations) is how certain US citizens and residents who are officers, directors, or shareholders in foreign corporations satisfy the reporting requirements of Internal Revenue Code sections 6038 and 6046. For Indian-origin US residents who founded, inherited, or still hold shares in an India private limited company (or group of related companies), this form is one of the most commonly missed international information returns — and one of the most expensive to miss. The Instructions for Form 5471 (revised December 2025) confirm a $10,000 penalty for each annual accounting period of each foreign corporation for failure to furnish the information required by section 6038(a) within the time prescribed, with additional $10,000 increments after IRS notice (capped) and a separate FTC haircut. Educational only — not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: US citizens and green-card / substantial-presence residents who (1) founded or still own an India Pvt Ltd (startup, consulting firm, family holding company, or operating business), (2) are officers or directors of a foreign corporation when another US person crosses a 10% ownership threshold (Category 2), (3) acquired, disposed of, or became a US person while holding ≥10% (Category 3), (4) control the company — more than 50% of vote or value — as a Category 4 filer, or (5) are a ≥10% US shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation (CFC) as a Category 5 filer. A CFC generally means US shareholders own more than 50% of vote or value on any day of the foreign corporation’s tax year. Family attribution under section 958 can stack siblings/parents/spouse ownership into CFC status even when no single person owns a majority.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: Attach a separate Form 5471 (and the schedules your category requires) to your US income tax return and file both by the due date including extensions. Category 4 (control >50% vote or value at any time during your tax year) and Category 5a (US shareholder of a CFC who owned the stock on the last day it was a CFC) are the heavy lifts: they typically pull in Schedules C/F/H/I/I-1/J/M/P/Q/R and can surface Subpart F and GILTI inclusions on your Form 1040 even if the India company never declared a dividend. Category 2/3 focus more on ownership-change reporting via Schedule O. Dormant companies may use the Rev. Proc. 92-70 summary procedure (page 1 only, labeled accordingly) — still a filing, not a free pass. Items reported on Form 5471 generally need not be duplicated on Form 8938 (FATCA), but FBAR (FinCEN 114) is a separate Bank Secrecy Act filing if foreign financial accounts exceed the threshold.

sections.heading: India-angle: Pvt Ltd + family attribution
sections.body: An India private limited company is a foreign corporation for US tax purposes. Typical traps: (1) you left India on H-1B/L-1/green card but kept founder shares or a nominee stake in the old Pvt Ltd; (2) parents/siblings in India hold the rest of the stock and constructive ownership under section 958(b) / section 318 principles pushes you over Category 4 control or makes the company a CFC with you as a Category 5 US shareholder; (3) you are an unpaid director on paper for the family company and a US person acquires ≥10%, triggering Category 2; (4) the company looks dormant (no employees, one bank account) so you assume no US filing — Rev. Proc. 92-70 still wants a labeled summary Form 5471. Separately, if the company is a CFC, Schedule I / Form 8992 territory can produce Subpart F or GILTI income inclusions that are taxable on your US return even when India taxes the company differently and you took no cash. Pair this with last week’s treaty Article 4 and Form 1116 thinking only after the information return is scoped — Form 5471 is disclosure first.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: List every India (or other foreign) corporation where you are a shareholder, officer, or director. For each, jot direct + family-attributed vote and value percentages and whether US persons together own more than 50%. If any Category 2–5 box might apply, calendar Form 5471 with your 2026 return (or extension) and bring the cap table to a cross-border CPA before year-end — do not wait for a K-1-style slip from India, because none will arrive.

India Pvt Ltd founder/family shares + section 958 attribution are a classic miss; dormant entities may still need Rev. Proc. 92-70 summary filing.

cards.title: Deep work beats shallow busywork
cards.body: Distraction-free focus creates hard-to-copy value. Shallow tasks feel productive but rarely move the needle — protect depth on purpose.
cards.source: Cal Newport · Deep Work (via mgp book-notes)

detail.summary: Newport's claim: deep work (distraction-free concentration at your cognitive limit) is getting rarer and more valuable. People who make it the core of how they work learn faster and produce things that are hard to copy. Shallow work is logistical, often distracted, and easy to replicate.

sections.heading: What deep work is
sections.body: Deep work is professional activity done with undivided attention — the kind that stretches your skills and creates new value. Shallow work is emailing, coordinating, and other low-cognition tasks you can do while half-distracted. Both exist; only one compounds skill.

sections.heading: Why it matters now
sections.body: Network tools slice attention into slivers, so most knowledge workers lose the habit of depth. That gap is the opportunity: if deep work is rare and valuable, the people who still protect it thrive. You do not need more hours; you need fewer interruptions during the hours that count.

sections.heading: Try today
sections.body: Block one 60–90 minute deep-work window. Pick one hard task (learning, writing, planning money rules — not inbox). Silence notifications, close chat, and treat the block like a meeting with yourself. One protected session beats a day of fragmented busyness.

bullets: Deep work: distraction-free focus that pushes your cognitive limit
Shallow work: easy, logistical, often distracted — low unique value
Hypothesis: depth is rarer and more valuable, so protect it on purpose

cards.title: Bedrock prompt caching: put cachePoint where context repeats
cards.body: Same long system prompt, tool schemas, or document across many Converse turns? Drop a cachePoint after the static prefix so later calls read cacheWrite-priced tokens as cheap cache reads (up to ~90% off input on hits). Prefer Converse over InvokeModel for model-agnostic markers; watch TTL and CRIS write churn.
cards.source: AWS ML Blog · Sep 15, 2026 · Bedrock User Guide

detail.summary: Amazon Bedrock prompt caching lets you mark reusable prompt prefixes so subsequent Converse (or ConverseStream) requests skip reprocessing that prefix. The Sep 15, 2026 AWS ML Blog walks six Converse patterns: message/document caching, system-prompt caching, tool-definition caching, mixed TTL (1h then 5m), SHA-256 tenant isolation, and LangChain ChatBedrockConverse.create_cache_point(). Explicit caching uses a cachePoint block after static content; implicit caching (where supported) tries prefix reuse without markers. Cache scope is per AWS account and Region. Checkpoints must meet model minimums (for example Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6 often need ≥1,024 tokens before a checkpoint). Default TTL is 5 minutes; many Claude models also support 1h. On hits, cacheReadInputTokens are billed far below standard input; first writes use cacheWriteInputTokens (higher than standard; 1h TTL writes cost more). Educational SA brief — confirm live pricing and model cards before you design for production.

sections.heading: Why SAs should care
sections.body: Agent and RAG apps repeatedly send the same system instructions, tool JSON schemas, and large reference blobs while only the user turn changes. Without caching you pay full input price every hop. Prompt caching is an infrastructure lever: keep prompt quality, cut TTFT on large prefixes, and shrink the input bill on cache hits — without shortening context into a thinner prompt. Pair it with Guardrails for safety; caching does not replace policy controls.

sections.heading: Where to place cachePoint
sections.body: Converse accepts cachePoint in three places, processed tools → system → messages. (1) Messages: put the static document/image blocks, then {"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}, then the changing question. (2) System: append cachePoint after a long persona/policy system array. (3) Tools: append cachePoint as the last entry in toolConfig.tools after all toolSpec entries. Claude on Bedrock also supports simplified management: one breakpoint after static content can look back across roughly ~20 prior content blocks for the longest matching prefix.

sections.heading: TTL, CRIS, and metrics
sections.body: Default TTL is 5m; set "ttl": "1h" on supported models for longer sessions (longer TTL checkpoints must appear before shorter ones in the same request). Cross-Region inference profiles can increase cache-write frequency under load — plan for occasional re-writes. Response usage exposes cacheWriteInputTokens and cacheReadInputTokens; with caching enabled, inputTokens is only the non-cached slice. Total input ≈ inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens. On ConverseStream, usage often arrives in the terminal metadata event. Log hit ratio; low hits usually mean the prefix mutates or TTL is too short.

sections.heading: Multi-tenant and agent tips
sections.body: Cache entries are account/Region scoped, not tenant scoped. For multi-tenant apps in one account, prepend a SHA-256 of tenant_id to the cached instructions (~16 tokens) so each tenant gets a separate prefix. For agents, cache tool schemas and system instructions once per TTL window; leave real-time user/tool results outside the checkpoint. Prefer Converse cachePoint over InvokeModel’s model-specific cache_control when you want the same code across Claude and Nova. On-demand only — batch inference does not support prompt caching.

sections.heading: Try this week
sections.body: In a non-prod Region, enable a caching-capable model (e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.5), run two Converse calls that share a ≥1,024-token document prefix with a cachePoint between document and question, and confirm request 1 shows cacheWriteInputTokens while request 2 shows cacheReadInputTokens. Then append cachePoint after a realistic toolConfig and measure agent-turn input cost before/after.

cards.title: Bedrock KB: Salesforce + Zendesk native sync
cards.body: Managed Knowledge Bases can now crawl Salesforce knowledge articles and Zendesk help/community posts natively (What's New Sep 23)—no custom ingest pipeline. OAuth + Secrets Manager, incremental sync, filters. SA timing: new Confluence/SharePoint/Salesforce/Web Crawler connectors on customer-managed KBs stop Sep 30, 2026; prefer Managed KB for those sources.
cards.source: AWS What's New · Bedrock User Guide · Sep 23, 2026

detail.summary: On Sep 23, 2026 AWS announced native Salesforce and Zendesk data source connectors for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. You hand over instance credentials (OAuth via Secrets Manager); the connector handles crawling, metadata extraction, and incremental sync so RAG apps stay current without a home-grown ingest pipeline. Use cases called out by AWS: customer support bots grounded in Zendesk help + community answers, and internal sales enablement assistants that retrieve Salesforce knowledge articles. Separately, docs warn that starting Sep 30, 2026, creating new Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, and Web Crawler connectors on customer-managed knowledge bases is no longer supported—existing ones keep working—so new work that needs those sources should target Managed Knowledge Base.

sections.heading: Why it matters for SA work
sections.body: RAG architecture questions often hinge on whether you build a custom crawler (Lambda + EventBridge + S3 + OpenSearch) or use a managed connector. Native Salesforce/Zendesk connectors shrink operational overhead and map cleanly to Well-Architected reliability and cost trade-offs—especially when the knowledge already lives in those systems of record. The Sep 30 customer-managed cutoff makes Managed KB the default path for new Salesforce (and related) connectors.

sections.heading: What syncs
sections.body: Salesforce: knowledge articles and related CRM content types the connector can crawl (with inclusion/exclusion pattern filters). Zendesk: help center articles (optional attachments) and community posts, optionally scoped by category/section IDs, community topic IDs, and label names. Both support incremental syncs for added, updated, and deleted content after the first full crawl.

sections.heading: Auth and IAM pattern
sections.body: Store OAuth client credentials in AWS Secrets Manager in the same Region as the knowledge base. Salesforce Connected App uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials (consumer key/secret; Run As user configured). Zendesk uses OAuth 2.0 with clientId, clientSecret, and instanceUrl in the secret. Grant the knowledge base IAM role Secrets Manager + connector permissions; prefer least privilege and rotate secrets regularly. Do not reuse one secret across unrelated data sources.

sections.heading: Permissions and PII caveats
sections.body: Anything synced becomes retrievable by principals with bedrock:Retrieve on that knowledge base—including content that had tighter controls in the source system. Zendesk docs note no document-level access control on crawled content. Salesforce crawl can include Case/Contact/Lead fields with personal data—use exclusion filters. Salesforce connector (customer-managed path) notes: preview caveats may apply, no multimodal tables/charts, and historically OpenSearch Serverless as the vector store pairing—confirm current Managed KB store options in the console for your Region.

sections.body: In a non-prod account, create a Managed Knowledge Base, add a Zendesk or Salesforce data source with a Secrets Manager secret pointing at a low-sensitivity sandbox, run one sync, then Retrieve with a few real support/sales questions. Compare latency and answer grounding vs your current PDF/S3 corpus before planning a migration off a custom crawler.

cards.title: India–US treaty Article 4: dual-resident tie-breaker
cards.body: Resident of both India and the US under domestic law (green card + India ROR, or substantial presence + Indian residential status)? Article 4 of the India–US income tax treaty cascades permanent home → centre of vital interests → habitual abode → nationality to assign one treaty residence. Claiming India under the treaty usually means Form 1040-NR + Form 8833 — and the saving clause still lets the US tax its citizens worldwide. Educational only, not tax advice.
cards.source: IRS · Tax treaties · Form 8833 · India–US treaty Art. 4

detail.summary: If you are a resident of the United States under IRC §7701(b) (green card or substantial presence) and also a resident of India under the Income-tax Act, 1961, you are a dual-resident taxpayer. Article 4 of the Convention between the United States and India for the Avoidance of Double Taxation (signed 1989, in force 1990) supplies a tie-breaker so you are treated as a resident of only one country for treaty purposes. The cascade is: permanent home available → closer personal and economic relations (centre of vital interests) → habitual abode → nationality → mutual agreement of the competent authorities. Dual residents who claim treaty residence of India for US return purposes generally file Form 1040-NR and attach Form 8833 (treaty-based return position). Article 1(3) (the saving clause) still lets the United States tax its citizens — and, subject to narrow exceptions in Article 1(4), its residents — as if the Convention had not come into effect. Educational only — not tax advice.

sections.heading: Who this helps
sections.body: Indian-origin green-card holders and long-stay workers who also meet India’s residential-status tests (for example ordinary resident / resident and ordinarily resident when days in India plus prior-year history stack up), dual homeowners with flats in India and the US, returning NRIs who keep a US green card while rebuilding an India life, and H-1B / L-1 workers who tip into substantial presence while still filing as Indian tax residents. US citizens who are dual residents should model this carefully: the saving clause usually preserves US worldwide taxation even if the tie-breaker points to India.

sections.heading: Rough mechanics
sections.body: First confirm dual residence under each country’s domestic law. Then apply Article 4(2) in order: (a) the Contracting State where you have a permanent home available; if both, the State with which your personal and economic relations are closer (centre of vital interests — family, social ties, occupation, political/cultural activities, place of business, property administration); (b) if that cannot be determined, or you have no permanent home in either State, habitual abode; (c) if habitual abode in both or neither, the State of which you are a national; (d) otherwise the competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement. If you claim to be a resident of India (not the United States) under the treaty for figuring US income tax, IRS guidance says file a timely Form 1040-NR and attach a fully completed Form 8833 disclosing the treaty-based return position under §6114 / Reg. §301.7701(b)-7. You are treated as a nonresident alien for figuring US tax, while other residency timing rules for alien status can still apply outside that computation.

sections.heading: India-angle: saving clause + what still helps
sections.body: Article 1(3) is the saving clause: notwithstanding most of the Convention, the United States may tax its residents (as determined under Article 4) and, by reason of citizenship, its citizens as if the Convention had not come into effect. Article 1(4) carves back limited benefits (for example certain associated-enterprise adjustments, private pensions/annuities/alimony/child support paragraphs, relief from double taxation, non-discrimination, mutual agreement, plus student/teacher articles for people who are neither citizens nor immigrants of the taxing State). Practically: a US citizen dual resident rarely escapes worldwide US taxation via Article 4 alone; a green-card holder who is not a citizen and whose centre of vital interests clearly sits in India may have a stronger case to claim India treaty residence with Form 8833 — still a facts-and-circumstances call. Either way, keep Form 1116 foreign tax credit and India’s own residential-status rules in the model, and do not confuse treaty residence with immigration status.

sections.heading: Check-this action
sections.body: Before year-end planning, list where you have a permanent home available, where your family and main economic ties sit, and your nationality(ies). If you are dual resident and considering an India treaty-residence claim, sketch Form 1040-NR vs Form 1040 outcomes with Form 8833 disclosure, and confirm whether the saving clause blocks the position (especially if you are a US citizen). Bring that one-pager to a cross-border CPA — do not file Form 8833 casually.

detail.summary: On Sep 22, 2026 AWS made OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna generally available on Amazon Bedrock, expanding the GPT-6 family alongside Astra. Sol targets recurring complex work (coding, debug, multistep tools); Luna targets high-volume focused tasks (extraction, summarization, classification, routing) with adjustable reasoning effort. Both support up to 1M tokens of context and explicit prompt caching on Bedrock, at significantly lower API pricing than their GPT-5.6 predecessors.
